t.4125534c: Hi, I'm Matthias, the creator of Zitro — a developer, a maker, and a father of three. Like most parents, I live the tension every day: I want to protect my kids from the overwhelming digital world, and at the same time I don't want to lock them out of it. They should grow up educated about AI — seeing its potential for creativity, knowledge, and agility, and learning its limits first-hand.
t.ef36b5be: Zitro is my answer to that tension: a device that answers their questions and then hands the moment back. No feed, no account, nothing pulling them in deeper. Curiosity in, an honest answer out, and eyes back on the world.
t.951cee9b: It started as an experiment at the intersection of hardware and software — "what if your AI assistant could fit in your pocket and work anywhere?" — and turned into something my own kids reach for. I hope it brings your family as much joy and curiosity as it brings ours.

t.c86eab18: Zitro for young minds — AI literacy through practice
t.342ece34: Kids will grow up with AI either way. Zitro lets them practise it early — asking, checking, steering — without a feed, an account, or an algorithm farming their curiosity.
t.52b8d1f5: Children are born curious. They ask why forty times a day. The phone is very good at catching that curiosity — and then keeping it, turning one question into an hour.
t.45d6352f: Zitro is built around a different instinct: answer the curiosity, then give the moment back. A kid asks why the moon follows the car, reads the answer, and looks back up at the moon — not down at a screen.
t.ab0687c6: Along the way, something bigger happens. Through small, everyday moments, kids build a working sense of what AI is: powerful, fallible, steerable, made by people — not magic. The lessons are never spoken as lessons. They live in how the device is used.
t.3b67e8f8: "Is that really true?" is a question you're allowed to ask a machine. The sentence comes from the AI and can be wrong; the photo next to it comes from Wikipedia. So the sentence gets checked: in a book, or with a grown-up.
t.7e9054b7: A found photo with a name under it is different from an invented picture. A Wolfram graph is different from a guess. Kids learn to tell them apart.
t.73fb1b54: "No — make the dragon scared of being too bright!" Generative AI as a collaborator you direct, not an oracle that decides.
t.b79d6236: Math shows worked steps on a tiny screen — nothing to copy-paste, no "regenerate". The device helps you learn the step, not skip it.
t.5c39fd02: Translations to hold up and point at. When the AI's wording comes out stiff, a human laughs and says it properly — and that's the lesson.
t.a1bd6bdf: Shake for one fact — octopuses have three hearts — then nothing slides in after it. You decide when there's a next one.
t.9b9d4678: Dusk. A kid and a parent walk home. The moon hangs over the rooftops and keeps pace with them. "Why is the moon following us?" — said out loud.
t.cbc29361: Zitro shows a sentence a seven-year-old gets: it isn't following; it's just so far away that it doesn't seem to move. The kid reads it, then asks the better question — "is that really true?" The little photo of the Moon from Wikipedia can't answer that: a photo shows the Moon, not why it seems to follow you. So at home they look it up together in the children's encyclopedia. Answer, then checking, then the kid is looking back up at the actual sky.
t.609a711d: The AI writes the answer, people check it — and the AI hands the curiosity back, instead of keeping it.
t.8fdba20a:
Guardrails parents
don't have to fight for
t.9ebc9f2a: When on, the device sleeps between 20:00 and 06:00. No bedtime negotiations with a gadget.
t.9d0c0b2f: No wake word, no ambient recording. It hears your kid only while the button is pressed.
t.0aedbb30: No child account, no profile. Zitro runs on the family's own AI key over the family's own network. The question goes to the AI service you pick, for example Infomaniak in Switzerland. Voice, read-aloud and pictures go to OpenAI for now; from the next update, Infomaniak can transcribe the voice too.
t.c94ec441: No feed, no notifications, no ads, no social layer, no infinite scroll. There is nothing pulling for re-engagement.
t.0b2b031d: The answer sits on a small shared screen — easy to read over a shoulder, easy to talk about at the table.
t.5538279a: The firmware is inspectable by anyone — including you. No black box between your kid and their questions.
t.29f05483: Across all of it, the same quiet shape repeats: ask → get an honest answer → look back at the world. The kid is always the one in charge — choosing to ask, choosing to check, choosing to steer, choosing when there's a next.
t.9c9ea291: They come away having learned two things at once: a fact about octopuses or the moon, and a habit — that AI is a powerful, fallible tool you point at a question and then put down. That habit is the most valuable thing Zitro teaches.
